generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, reflective practice is not an optional study habit; it is built into how the profession develops and regulates itself. Trainee and qualified psychologists are expected to reflect on their practice continually, in supervision, in appraisal and in the records a professional body requires. The point is development: looking back critically at how you handled an assessment, a session or a decision, judging it against the standards of the discipline, and changing what you do. Reflection is the evaluation phase of a psychologist's own self-regulation.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two trainee psychologists reflecting on the same difficult placement episode, a first assessment session that did not go to plan.

Tom writes the episode up because the placement portfolio requires it. His account sets out what happened, in order, and notes that he felt out of his depth but that the session finished acceptably. It is honest and complete, but Tom treats reflection as a task to discharge: he does not ask why the session went as it did, weighs nothing against the standards he is training toward, and changes nothing as a result. For Tom, reflection is compliance.

Amara writes the same episode up as a professional examining her own practice. She asks why she rushed the rapport-building, weighs her choices against what the discipline expects of an assessment, and connects her discomfort to her limited preparation rather than the client. She reaches a specific conclusion, to structure her next assessment differently, and commits to it. For Amara, the episode becomes development.

Both trainees reflected. Only Amara treated reflection as professional practice, using it to understand herself and improve.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, reflective practice is the engine of a practitioner's self-regulated development: the evaluation phase in which you look back critically at your own practice against the standards of the discipline, and keep doing so across a career in supervision, appraisal and professional records. You can now articulate why it matters, appraise how well a trainee reflects, and judge what owning it demands of you. The next lesson gives you Kolb's cycle as a structure for reflecting critically on a single experience.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection professional practice rather than compliance?

items.text: She weighed her own choices against the standards of the discipline and committed to a specific change.
She produced a longer and more detailed account of the session.
She completed the placement portfolio entry on time.
She described exactly what happened in the session, in order.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing her practice against the discipline's standards and committing to a change is reflection as development.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did beyond recording the session.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's reflection was professional practice because she weighed her choices against the discipline's standards and committed to a change, not because it was longer, on time or well ordered.
